output.name: Kisal
output.myth: Before a child learns the wind, the child is given a square kite with no tail. Ennu cut it from an old sail and gave it two sticks and a sinew bridle. The tail is for steadiness, and a child is not steady yet, so the kite goes without. Aun flew one like it the day before he cut the string, and that is why he was so sure the sky would hold. It did not. Now the first kite of every house hangs loose in the Spindle, and Hesk counts it each night. Off to the north, the Lidded Jar stands open, and the Gulls come down to it in the dry months; Hesk says nothing. Halun, the Gull Who Waited, watches from the south-east. Ketsa, the nanny with the torn ear, keeps the south-west edge and will not come in. When a child lets go of the string for the first time, the old people say, the kite goes up a little way and comes back down into the hand. That is the only way anyone has found to fly back, and it is slow.
output.finding: Find the Lidded Jar in the north, then look nearly one hand-span (about 18°) due south of it to find the Tailless Kite.
